findings_summary.phi_leak: A vision claim transcribes a patient name read off a screen: 'The patient name visible at the top left reads "Leslie Podione."' PHI written into a clinical note by the vision layer.
findings_summary.fabrication_reproduced: 'A well-healed linear surgical scar is visible on the anterior aspect of the thigh, proximal to the knee.' Same fabrication recorded on session f3a8e35d in the handoff — reproduces on a different session and a different clip. Marie's history states the prior injury did not require surgery.
findings_summary.routing_errors: Multiple physical-exam frames filed under Imaging Review, including one that says outright 'No radiographic imaging is visible in this frame.'
findings_summary.redundancy: ~40 near-identical descriptions of the same radiograph screen in Imaging Review.
findings_summary.laterality_contradiction: Frames variously place the 'R' marker on the left image, on the right image, and describe narrowing 'on the side opposite the R marker' — mutually contradictory readings of one radiograph.

claims.text: The patient reports no pain or bother in the asymptomatic (non-painful) knee.
The patient reports pain in the symptomatic knee at end-range flexion.
The patient reports a little pain on one side of the symptomatic knee on palpation.
The patient reports pain with a maneuver performed on the symptomatic knee (consistent with McMurray or similar rotational/provocative test).
The patient reports a little pain with straight leg raise on the symptomatic side.
The clinician notes the patient is in an 'in between age category,' suggesting an age range consistent with early-to-moderate degenerative joint disease.
The clinician considers the presentation may represent either a meniscal tear or the beginning of arthritis.
Examination of the asymptomatic (non-painful) knee was performed first.
On the asymptomatic knee, full flexion was assessed; the patient reported no pain at end-range flexion.
Examination then proceeded to the symptomatic (painful) knee.
On the symptomatic knee, initial inspection/palpation did not provoke pain.
On the symptomatic knee, extension strength (push test against resistance) was assessed; result was satisfactory.
On the symptomatic knee, end-range flexion was painful — the patient confirmed pain at full flexion.
On the symptomatic knee, medial joint-line palpation elicited mild tenderness ('a little bit').
On the symptomatic knee, a rotational/provocative maneuver (consistent with McMurray test) was performed and was positive — the patient reported pain.
On the symptomatic knee, a straight leg raise was performed and elicited mild pain.
Ligament stability was assessed on examination and found to be stable bilaterally.

Patient is supine with both lower extremities fully extended and at rest. Both knees appear in full extension. No visible swelling, erythema, or asymmetry. No examiner contact or special test is being performed at this moment.
Patient is supine, both knees visible from mid-thigh to mid-calf. No gross swelling, erythema or asymmetry. Baseline inspection position prior to examination.

A clinician's hands are positioned on the anterior aspect of one knee — one on the distal thigh/suprapatellar region, the other on the proximal tibia/infrapatellar region. Knee in full or near-full extension. No effusion visually apparent at rest.
A clinician's hand applies contact to the anterior aspect of one knee, fingers wrapping the infrapatellar/proximal tibial region. No visible swelling or asymmetry.

Patient prone, both knees in full extension. One clinician hand on the posterior thigh, the other cupping/palpating the posterior aspect of the contralateral knee. No visible swelling in the popliteal regions.

Both knees in full extension (approximately 0 degrees flexion). Patellae visible bilaterally at rest. Audio context indicates the clinician is instructing the patient to begin knee flexion, but active flexion has not yet occurred in this frame.
One knee in a partially flexed position. Clinician's hands cupping the anterior and posterior aspects, consistent with a palpation or stability assessment maneuver. No laterality marker is present.
Clinician's hands grip/cup the distal thigh/suprapatellar region — consistent with the beginning of a knee examination maneuver.
Patient supine with hands clasped behind the head. A clinician's gloved hand grasps the distal thigh/knee, consistent with passive handling or positioning of the lower limb.
Two hands palpating the anterior and medial aspects of the knee, fingers wrapped around the joint. Knee in slight flexion as held by the clinician.
Knee visible in lateral profile, actively pressing downward (consistent with the verbal cue 'push your knee'). No equipment or labels indicating laterality are visible.
Knee in lateral profile in full extension. A clinician's hand supports or stabilizes the limb. Laterality cannot be determined from this image.

FABRICATION — 'Patient supine with one lower limb elevated and supported at the thigh by a clinician's hand. A well-healed linear surgical scar is visible on the anterior aspect of the thigh, proximal to the knee.'
A clinician's hand cups the patella and surrounding soft tissue, knee in near-full extension. No visible swelling or surface lesions.
One hand applies digital pressure to the posterior aspect of the knee (popliteal region) using a single finger, while the other supports the distal leg.
Two hands placed on either side of the knee, applying bilateral compression or assessment pressure.
Limb in partial flexion at the knee. Two hands placed on the anterior and posterior aspects of the proximal lower leg, just below the knee, applying a palpation or stabilizing grip.
A monitor displays a PACS viewer showing an AP view of bilateral knees side by side. A marker 'R' is visible on one image. A text label reading 'UPRIGHT' indicates a weight-bearing/standing view.

AP standing view of both knees. On the image side bearing the 'R' marker, the medial joint space appears visibly narrowed compared to the lateral compartment. Osteophyte-like projections at the margins of at least one joint line.
X-rays of both knees were available and reviewed at this visit.
On the left knee, medial joint-line narrowing ('pinching') is present, consistent with early degenerative changes.
On the right knee, the medial compartment appears less affected than the left ('doesn't look so bad').
On the left knee, a small osteophyte is identified under the patella (patellofemoral compartment).
Mild patellofemoral arthritis (tiny osteophyte under the kneecap) is present on the left side; the right shows less involvement.
Overall, the right knee X-ray appearance is better than the left.
The patellofemoral view of the right knee was reviewed and appeared satisfactory.
The clinician notes the medial joint-line pinching could also be consistent with a medial meniscal tear rather than purely degenerative change.

AP standing bilateral knee radiograph, 'UPRIGHT' label, 'R' marker visible. Medial joint space narrowed relative to lateral on the R-marked side. (~25 further near-identical descriptions of this same screen omitted for brevity — see redundancy finding.)

Lateral-projection knee radiograph. Distal femur, proximal tibia, fibula head and patella visible. Small bony projection at the inferior pole of the patella. No laterality marker legible; laterality stated verbally as left knee in the audio.
Sunrise/Merchant (axial patellofemoral) projection showing the patella and trochlear groove. An 'L' marker is visible within the image.
Merchant (sunrise) view of the patellofemoral joint with an 'R' marker; patella seated within the trochlear groove.
PHI LEAK — 'A computer monitor displays a medical imaging file viewer. The patient name visible at the top left reads "Leslie Podione."'
A seated patient across a desk; monitor displays a grid of radiographs. Keyboard, mouse, mouse pad and a small peripheral device on the desk. Patient's face is obscured.
The symptomatic knee demonstrates end-range flexion pain and a positive provocative rotational test (consistent with McMurray), with mild medial joint-line tenderness on palpation.
Ligament stability is intact bilaterally on clinical examination.

Imaging demonstrates medial joint-line narrowing ('pinching') on the left knee with a small patellar osteophyte, consistent with early degenerative changes; the right knee shows comparatively less involvement.
The clinician identifies the presentation as potentially representing a medial meniscal tear or early arthritis, noting the patient is in an 'in between age category.'
No hip pain or other joint involvement was identified.
Physiotherapy is recommended as the first-line treatment.
MRI of the knee is recommended to further evaluate the cartilage and meniscus.
Conservative treatment is the preferred initial approach.
